title: How do energy companies and utilities make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Energy and utilities economics for case interviews: regulated returns, generation costs, capacity, the energy transition and rooftop solar, with a worked…
hook: Energy companies make money in three quite different ways: generators sell the electricity they produce, network owners earn a regulated return on the grid they build, and retailers earn a thin margin selling energy to homes and businesses. In an energy case, first work out which of these the client is, then focus on the long-lived investment decisions, the regulation and the price and weather risks that drive that part of the value chain.
body:
The three businesses

BusinessHow it earns moneyWhat drives profit
GenerationSells electricity from gas, wind, solar, nuclear and moreOutput, realised price, fuel and operating cost, capital cost
NetworksCharges for moving power over the grid, usually as a regulated monopolySize of the asset base, the allowed return, performance incentives
RetailBuys energy wholesale and sells it to customersCustomer churn, acquisition cost, buying energy below what contracts recover

Some companies do all three, but they still earn money differently in each, so analyse them separately.

Generation: capacity is not output

A power plant's nameplate capacity (in megawatts, MW) is its maximum output. What it actually produces over a year depends on its capacity factor: actual output divided by what it would produce running flat out all year. Wind and solar depend on the weather, so their capacity factors are well below 100%.

Take an illustrative 100 MW wind farm with a 35% capacity factor, selling at $65 per megawatt-hour (MWh). There are 8,760 hours in a year.

  • Output: 100 MW × 8,760 hours × 35% = 306,600 MWh.
  • Revenue: 306,600 × $65 ≈ $19.9M a year, before operating costs and financing.
  • At a 30% capacity factor, output is 262,800 MWh and revenue about $17.1M: a $2.85M drop from a windier or calmer site.

Because the plant is almost all upfront cost and lasts decades, the decision is an investment case: does the stream of cash over 25 or more years justify the capital today? That is where payback and NPV come in. Generators can sell at the wholesale market price (and take the price risk) or lock in a fixed price for years with a power purchase agreement.

Networks: regulated returns

Grids are natural monopolies, so in many countries a regulator sets what they may charge. Broadly, the regulator lets the owner recover its operating costs and depreciation and earn an allowed return on its asset base. If an illustrative network has a $10B asset base and an allowed return of 6%, it earns about $600M of return. Investing another $1B in approved upgrades adds about $60M a year. So a regulated network grows profit by growing its approved asset base and beating the regulator's performance targets, not by selling more electricity.

Retail: thin margins and price risk

Suppose a retailer sells to a household on a fixed price of 20 cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh). Wholesale energy costs 9 cents, network charges 7 cents and its own costs 3 cents, leaving 1 cent of margin. If wholesale prices jump to 11 cents and the retailer had not bought ahead (hedged), it now loses 1 cent on every kWh. On a household using 3,000 kWh a year, a $30 profit becomes a $30 loss. That is how retailers fail when wholesale prices spike.

Rooftop solar and the utility

A utility sells 10,000 gigawatt-hours (GWh) a year to homes. If 10% of homes install solar panels and cut their grid use by 40%, sales fall by 10% × 40% = 4%, or 400 GWh. But the grid still has to serve those homes at night. If $1.2B of network costs are recovered per unit sold, the charge rises from 12 cents to 12.5 cents per kWh (about 4%) for everyone else, which pushes more customers towards solar. Each part of the value chain is affected differently: networks face cost recovery problems, retailers lose volume but can sell panels, batteries and flexibility services.

Typical energy case questions

  • Should we build a wind farm, and should we sell at market prices or sign a fixed-price contract?
  • Should a company put solar on its roof or buy power from a developer?
  • Should we replace gas boilers with heat pumps? (an investment case)
  • How should a utility respond to rooftop solar?

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "A 100 MW wind farm produces 100 MW, so at $65 that's a lot of revenue."
Strong: "At a 35% capacity factor the farm produces about 307,000 MWh a year, roughly $20M at $65. Since almost all the cost is upfront, I'd want the price we can lock in and the cost of capital before judging the NPV."

Common mistakes

  • Treating capacity as output. Always apply a capacity factor.
  • Ignoring which part of the value chain the client owns. Rooftop solar is a threat to one part and an opportunity for another.
  • Forgetting regulation. For networks, the regulator decides much of the revenue.
  • Ignoring time. Assets last decades, so discounting, financing and policy risk matter more than in most cases.

Practise

1. A 50 MW solar farm has a 25% capacity factor and sells at $50 per MWh. What is its annual revenue?

Show the answer

Output: 50 × 8,760 × 25% = 109,500 MWh. Revenue: 109,500 × $50 ≈ $5.5M a year.

2. In the retail example, how much would wholesale prices have to rise before the retailer breaks even on its fixed-price contracts?

Show the answer

Margin is 1 cent per kWh, so a rise of 1 cent (from 9 to 10 cents, about 11%) wipes it out. A thin margin with unhedged price exposure is a fragile business.

3. A regulated network can invest $500M in approved grid upgrades at an allowed return of 6%. Why might it want to, even if electricity demand is flat?

Show the answer

Its profit comes from the asset base, not volumes: $500M × 6% = $30M a year of extra allowed return, provided the regulator approves the spend and the company delivers it within budget.

Where to practise next

Try the Arbor Wind case (market price or fixed contract), the Vega Logistics case (rooftop solar: own it or buy the power), the Northwind Hotels case (heat pumps versus boilers) and the Fenland Biogas case. The payback and NPV worked examples cover the maths.
